Date: 2026-05-27

Attendees: Sara Kim (Redwood AE), Diego Alvarez (Redwood SE), Maya Singh (Quantaco ML Eng), Tom Reynolds (Quantaco CTO), Lisa Chen (Quantaco PM)
summary: Weekly POC sync focused on cost/unit economics. Redwood presented updated tokens/sec/$ numbers across two model variants and showed caching and batching tradeoffs. Customer requested KV-cache microbenchmarks with 4k/8k sequences and to validate savings on their prompt sets. Agreed to share updated cost spreadsheet and schedule a dedicated-pool run. Action items assigned.
topics: Throughput and tokens/sec/$ for model variants
KV/prefix caching expected savings vs real-world prompts
Batching tradeoffs: latency SLO vs cost efficiency
Next steps: benchmarks, pricing sheet, prompt uploads
transcript: [00:00] Sara (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, happy Wednesday. quick check in on the cost econ work for the POC
[00:18] Tom (CTO): Thanks Sara, yeah we want to make sure the unit economics lines up before we scale beyond the pilot
[00:28] Diego (Redwood SE): we pushed the numbers up in the sheet — tokens per second per dollar — and included cache savings assumptions, i can walk through that
[00:40] Maya (ML): perfect, we care most about tokens/sec/$ for our high-fanout inference — mostly 2k-6k seqs — and cache hit rates on repeated prefixes
[00:55] Lisa (PM): timeline wise we want to decide by mid-june if Dedicated makes sense given cost vs hosted
[01:10] Sara: ok quick agenda: review updated numbers, discuss KV cache assumptions, batching impact on latency, and agree next steps

[01:28] Diego: slide 1, baseline numbers — model-gpt-3.8-ql (faster) and model-3.8-std (higher quality). for the fast variant we measured ~1,200 tokens/sec on A100-like hardware in our hosted profile, and for std about 680 tokens/sec
[01:58] Tom: those tokens/sec numbers assume no batching or continuous batching?

[02:05] Diego: it's with the default continuous batching we run on hosted; single-request latency was lower but throughput per dollar improves with batching. note our tokens/sec/$ calc folds in GPU utilization and amortized infra cost
[02:30] Maya: can you remind me how you're calculating tokens/sec/$? is that tokens per GPU-second over cost per GPU-hour translated to per-dollar?
[02:45] Diego: yes, basically tokens per second * 3600 gives tokens per GPU hour, divide by our per-hour cost to get tokens per dollar. then we adjust for batching inefficiencies and KV cache hits
[03:05] Lisa: okay and the cache savings numbers were optimistic in last week’s sheet — want to be conservative here

[03:15] Diego: understood. our latest run uses three cache-hit scenarios: 10%, 30%, 50% prefix hit. those change effective tokens/sec/$ significantly — at 30% hits the effective cost per 1M tokens drops about 28% for the fast variant
[03:40] Tom: that's big — but our prompts are long and only the first 400 tokens repeat across users, rest is context, so hit rates might be lower
[03:55] Maya: yep, most of our prompts have a shared system prompt and then variable user content. we saw about 20% real hit in our internal logs last month
[04:10] Sara: that's why Diego's proposing we run a KV-cache microbench with your real prompt sets to get realistic numbers — Diego?
[04:20] Diego: yeah i'll run microbench with 3 seed prompt sets Maya will upload; i'll run with seq=4k and 8k, and measure tokens/sec, p50/p95/p99 latency, and bytes to/from KV cache
[04:40] Maya: i'll upload them today — maybe a mix of long support conversations, code-gen prompts, and short search prompts
[04:50] Lisa: for batching tradeoffs, how do you recommend we approach latency SLOs? our product needs <350ms p95 for interactive flows

[05:05] Diego: batching gives big cost wins but increases tail latency. we can tune batch windows and then use dynamic routing: low-latency traffic bypasses big batches, background jobs use large batches. that's what our smart routing does
[05:30] Tom: any hard numbers for p95 at different batch sizes?

[05:35] Diego: rough rule: for that fast model, small batch sizes up to 8 keep p95 under 300ms for 1-2k seqs; larger batch sizes push p95 north of 400ms. exact depends on seq length. i'll provide a table
[06:00] Maya: curious about warm vs cold KV cache effects; if everyone hits different prefixes warms slowly

[06:10] Diego: hit — cold starts cost more. our runtime also supports prefix caching at the request layer and persistent KV cache per model variant. warmup benchmarks show most gains after 10-20 similar prefixes
[06:30] Sara: note that Dedicated pools let you pin warmed caches and get more predictable unit economics but require a commit
[06:42] Tom: commit risk is the main blocker for us on Dedicated — if we don't reach utilization, cost per token goes up
[06:52] Lisa: what's the minimum committed throughput for a cost advantage?

[06:57] Diego: depends on model; for the fast variant commit that sustains >60% utilization we usually show ~20-30% unit cost reduction vs hosted burstable, but it requires a monthly commitment. we'll model a few scales in the spreadsheet
[07:15] Sara: we've added a sensitivity table to the sheet showing cost per 1M tokens at 40/60/80% utilization and at 10/30/50% cache hits
[07:28] Maya: can you paste current numbers?

[07:32] Sara: quick snapshot — fast variant: $8.50 per 1M tokens at baseline no-cache, drops to $6.10 at 30% cache hits and 60% util; std variant: $12.40 -> $9.00. (transcription: numbers approximate)
[07:58] Tom: that delta between variants is significant; product team will likely pick fast variant if quality loss is acceptable
[08:10] Maya: what's the quality regression between fast and std? measured by our eval sets?

[08:18] Diego: we ran BLEU/ROUGE-like evals on your dev prompts — fast variant had a ~3% drop in some metrics for code-gen but was similar on short chat prompts. quality tuning and prompt-engineering can shrink gap
[08:40] Lisa: is quantization involved? earlier you mentioned ql suffix
[08:45] Diego: ql is our quantized-low variant, yes it's quantized for lower memory and slightly different perf profile. quantization helps pack more instances per GPU which improves tokens/sec/$
[09:00] Tom: any concerns about hallucination or fidelity with quantized models?
[09:06] Diego: there's a small uptick in hallucination risk on certain generative tasks; we'll surface specific failure modes in the eval report. tradeoff is cost per token

[09:25] Sara: circling back to batching — we propose hybrid: interactive endpoints pinned to small batch windows, bulk endpoints use aggressive batching. that gets you most of the cost wins without breaking p95 for interactive flows
[09:45] Maya: okay makes sense. do you have recommended defaults we can start with?
[09:50] Diego: yes: interactive batch window 20ms, max batch size 8; bulk batch window 200ms, max 64. those are starting points and we'll tune against your traffic
[10:10] Tom: curious re: network egress and storage costs? KV cache being external store increases ops cost, right?

[10:18] Diego: we account for KV store IO in the model but it's small relative to GPU. if you host KV close to runtime (same region/VPC) it's negligible. using managed Redis or our in-memory cache reduces roundtrip
[10:35] Lisa: security question: for Private/VPC deployments, how does key management and audit logs work?
[10:42] Sara: we support customer KMS, HSM integrations, and audit logs with retention config. we'll share the SOC2/ISO docs and network architecture note
[10:55] Tom: please do, legal will need that for the procurement packet
[11:00] Maya: back to numbers — i want to see the cost delta with your worst-case cache hit (10%) and best-case (50%) across both variants
[11:12] Diego: noted, i'll add percent deltas in the sheet. also i'll include p99 latency impacts for each batching config
[11:25] Sara: we should also show an example per-route configuration — interactive vs batch — and the estimated monthly bill for a sample workload you gave last week
[11:36] Maya: yes please. that sample workload is the 200 qps baseline with spiky peaks to 800 qps during business hours
[11:45] Diego: for spikes, smart routing can spill to higher-cost burst pool if dedicated capacity is saturated. that shows up in the cost model as a small tail spend
[12:00] Tom: what about fallback model chains for graceful degradation when capacity constrained?
[12:06] Diego: we support automated fallback to cheaper variants and region fallbacks. fallback quality must be validated against your success criteria — we'll include pass/fail triggers
[12:20] Lisa: what's the expected savings if we enable prefix caching plus batching vs just batching?
[12:26] Diego: example: with 30% prefix hits + batching tuned, combined you can see ~40% cost reduction compared to naive single-request served on std variant — but again depends on prompts
[12:45] Maya: ok, that's encouraging. however i want real numbers from our prompts not hypotheticals
[12:52] Sara: agreed — that's why we prioritized the KV-cache microbench and the dedicated run. metadata: we'll also mask PHI in prompts before upload
[13:05] Maya: done — i'll mask and upload tonight
[13:10] Diego: quick clarification: when you upload prompt sets, include frequency distribution of prefixes if you have it, helps caching sim
[13:20] Maya: i'll try to extract that from logs, might be noisy but we'll include best-effort
[13:30] Tom: on procurement: do you have a templated SOW or pricing tiers for Dedicated?
[13:36] Sara: yes we'll share a draft SOW and sample committed tiers. legal will follow after the technical sign-off
[13:45] Lisa: any open risks we should call out?
[13:50] Diego: risk: if hit rates remain low, Dedicated commit could underdeliver ROI — mitigation: start with smaller commit and use burst to cover demand; we can model a ramp
[14:05] Maya: also risk: quantized model quality might need extra prompt engineering which is engineer time cost on our side
[14:12] Sara: noted. we'll include an eng-effort estimate in the packet
[14:20] Diego: last technical note: latency measurement artifacts — make sure to measure end-to-end from your app through our SDK to capture network effects, not just the runtime internal latency
[14:35] Tom: good point, we'll run both internal and end-to-end tests during the dedicated run

[14:45] Sara: ok summarizing next steps: Diego runs KV-cache microbench (4k/8k) using Maya's prompt sets, Sara shares updated cost spreadsheet and draft SOW, Maya uploads prompts, schedule dedicated-pool run for early June
[15:00] Lisa: sounds good, i'll help coordinate dates from our side
[15:08] Tom: thanks all, looking forward to the numbers
[15:12] Sara: thanks everyone, i'll follow up after the call with links: cost sheet, SOW draft, and a calendar invite for the perf run
[15:20] Diego: bye
[15:22] Maya: bye
[15:23] Tom: bye
